specPoints.text: know that alcohols contain the functional group −OH

understand how to draw structural and displayed formulae for methanol, ethanol, propanol (propan-1-ol only) and butanol (butan-1-ol only), and name each compound the names propanol and butanol are acceptable

primer.text: From Bromine & Alkenes you already know how a functional group dictates a reaction test. This note closes the wave on a third functional group: the hydroxyl group of the alcohols, the family behind fuels and spirits, with the naming twist that trades a final e for an ol.

lessons.title: The hydroxyl group that defines the family
lessons.opening: Alcohols are colourless liquids that mix with water and burn as fuels. This lesson fixes the one feature that makes them a family: the hydroxyl group responsible for their characteristic reactions.
keyPoints: Alcohols are clear liquids that mix with water, giving neutral solutions.
The first four members of the family serve as common fuels.
Every alcohol carries the hydroxyl group, written -OH.
The hydroxyl group is the part of the molecule responsible for the characteristic reactions of alcohols.
In ethanol the -OH side chain is what characterises its chemistry, as the diagram of the molecule shows.

low.restatement: Alcohols are clear liquids that mix with water into neutral solutions and burn well as fuels. What makes them a family is the -OH hydroxyl group every member carries. Fuels and spirits alike belong to this one family.
low.analogy: The -OH group is a family badge worn by every alcohol; the carbon chain behind it may vary, but the badge decides how the whole family behaves.
low.examPointer: Write the functional group as -OH, and quote neutral solutions when describing their behaviour in water.

medium.restatement: Alcohols are colourless liquids dissolving in water to give neutral solutions, and the first four members serve as common fuels. Their shared feature is the hydroxyl functional group, -OH, the bonded arrangement that governs the characteristic reactions distinguishing alcohols from alkanes and alkenes.
medium.analogy: If the carbon chain is the furniture of the molecule, the -OH group is the mains socket: whatever the furniture, that socket decides which appliances, meaning reactions, can be plugged in.
medium.examPointer: Name the group and its consequence together: -OH present, therefore the characteristic alcohol reactions follow.

check.stem: Which functional group do all alcohols contain?

options.text: The hydroxyl group, -OH
options.explanation: The -OH arrangement is what every member of the alcohol family carries.

options.text: The C=C double bond
options.explanation: That defines the alkenes; alcohols are saturated apart from the OH group.

options.text: A carboxylic acid group
options.explanation: That stronger oxidation group belongs to a different family beyond this note.

options.text: A carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: Halogen bonds belong to the halogenoalkanes, not the alcohols.

check.stem: What is observed when an alcohol dissolves in water?

options.text: It forms a neutral solution
options.explanation: The note states alcohols dissolve in water to form neutral solutions.

options.text: It forms an acidic solution
options.explanation: Acidity belongs to the carboxylic acids, not the alcohols here.

options.text: It forms an alkaline solution
options.explanation: The hydroxyl group is covalently bonded, not ionic like alkali hydroxides.

options.text: It will not dissolve at all
options.explanation: Dissolving is exactly what the note records them doing.

check.stem: Why is the -OH group called the functional group of ethanol?

options.text: Because it is the part responsible for ethanol's characteristic reactions
options.explanation: The functional group is by definition the reactive arrangement steering the family chemistry.

options.text: Because it functions as the fuel itself
options.explanation: The whole molecule burns; the group name refers to reactive role, not fuel duty.

options.text: Because it adds the most mass to the molecule
options.explanation: Mass share is irrelevant to the functional group concept.

options.text: Because it was the first part discovered
options.explanation: Discovery order plays no part in the definition.

check.stem: Why are the first four alcohols commonly used?

options.text: As fuels, because they burn releasing energy
options.explanation: The note lists the first four alcohols as commonly used fuels.

options.text: As bleaches for fabrics
options.explanation: Bleaching is not among the listed uses.

options.text: As oxidising agents in engines
options.explanation: They are the burned substance, not the supplier of oxygen.

options.text: As indicators for acidity
options.explanation: They form neutral solutions, the opposite of indicator material.

check.stem: How do alcohols differ structurally from the alkanes they resemble?

options.text: One hydrogen is replaced by the hydroxyl group, -OH
options.explanation: The OH side chain replaces a hydrogen on the carbon chain, creating the new family.

options.text: Alcohols have a carbon-carbon double bond
options.explanation: That would make them alkenes; alcohol chains stay single-bonded.

options.text: Alcohols contain a metal atom
options.explanation: No metal appears in these molecular alcohols.

options.text: Alcohols have no hydrogen atoms at all
options.explanation: The OH group itself contains a hydrogen, and the chains carry many more.

lessons.title: The first four alcohols
lessons.opening: Naming alcohols reuses the alkane system with one letter swap. This lesson lines up methanol to butan-1-ol with their formulae and decodes what the number in the name records.
keyPoints: The first four alcohols are methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propan-1-ol C3H7OH and butan-1-ol C4H9OH.
Naming uses the alkane and alkene system with the final e replaced by ol.
Propanol and butanol are acceptable names for propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol in exams.
The 1 in propan-1-ol records that the -OH group sits on the first carbon atom.
Structural and displayed formulae show the OH group hanging on the carbon chain of each member.

low.restatement: Take the alkane name, drop the final e and add ol: methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol. The number says which carbon carries the OH, and short names propanol and butanol are accepted.
low.analogy: It is the alkane surname with a new ending swapped in, like a marriage certificate: same family line, new chemical identity announced by the ol.
low.examPointer: Either form, propan-1-ol or propanol, earns the mark, but draw the OH on the first carbon when the 1 is quoted.

medium.restatement: The homologous run runs methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propan-1-ol C3H7OH and butan-1-ol C4H9OH, named by replacing the alkane final e with ol. The position number fixes which carbon bears the OH group, the first carbon for the butan-1-ol of this course, and the shortened names propanol and butanol are acceptable.
medium.analogy: Think of the carbon chain as a numbered terrace of houses: the stem names the street, the suffix ol says a hydroxyl resident lives there, and the number gives the house where it moved in.
medium.examPointer: Draw the displayed formula with OH on the stated carbon, and remember the spec accepts propanol and butanol as names.

options.text: C2H5OH
options.explanation: The two-carbon alcohol carries five chain hydrogens plus the hydroxyl hydrogen.

options.text: CH3OH
options.explanation: That is methanol, the one-carbon member of the family.

options.text: C2H5COOH
options.explanation: That formula belongs to the acid family, not the alcohols.

options.text: C3H7OH
options.explanation: Three carbons is propan-1-ol, one rung above ethanol.

check.stem: How is the name of an alcohol built from the alkane name?

options.text: The final e of the alkane name is replaced with ol
options.explanation: Methane to methanol, ethane to ethanol: one letter swap records the OH group.

options.text: The stem is replaced with the word alcohol
options.explanation: The stem stays; only the ending changes.

options.text: The suffix ane is replaced with ene
options.explanation: That is the alkene rule; alcohols take the ol ending.

options.text: A prefix hydro- is added to the alkane name
options.explanation: No hydro- prefix exists in this system.

check.stem: What does the 1 in propan-1-ol record?

options.text: That the OH group sits on the first carbon atom
options.explanation: The number is the address of the hydroxyl group along the three-carbon chain.

options.text: That the molecule contains one carbon
options.explanation: The stem prop already fixes three carbons; the 1 locates the group.

options.text: That the alcohol is the first member of the family
options.explanation: Methanol is the first member; the number is about position, not order.

options.text: That one water molecule is attached
options.explanation: The OH is bonded into the molecule, not water stuck on.

check.stem: Which name is acceptable in the exam for propan-1-ol?

options.text: Propanol
options.explanation: The exam hint states the names propanol and butanol are acceptable.

options.text: Propane
options.explanation: That is the alkane with no OH group at all.

options.text: Propyl
options.explanation: Propyl is a fragment name, not the compound name.

options.text: Propanone
options.explanation: That belongs to the ketone family beyond this course.

check.stem: Which displayed formula correctly shows butan-1-ol?

options.text: A four-carbon chain with the OH group bonded to the end carbon
options.explanation: Butan-1-ol places the hydroxyl on carbon one of the four-carbon chain, as the table shows.

options.text: A three-carbon chain with OH in the middle
options.explanation: Both the chain length and the group position are wrong for butan-1-ol.

options.text: A four-carbon chain with a C=C double bond
options.explanation: A double bond would make it an alkene; alcohol chains are single-bonded.

options.text: A four-carbon chain with OH on every carbon
options.explanation: One hydroxyl group per molecule is the rule at this level.

glossary.definition: A member of the homologous series carrying the hydroxyl group, neutral in water and usable as fuels.
The -OH arrangement of atoms bonded to the carbon chain, responsible for the characteristic reactions of alcohols.
The one-carbon alcohol, CH3OH, the first member of the series.
The two-carbon alcohol, C2H5OH, whose molecule shows the OH side chain clearly.
The three-carbon alcohol, C3H7OH, with the OH group on the first carbon; propanol is acceptable.
